intro_text:
Cable Beach runs about four kilometers along Nassau's north shore on New Providence Island, named for a submarine telegraph cable that came ashore at Goodman's Bay, near its eastern end, in 1892 — the first cable linking the Bahamas to the United States, from Jupiter, Florida. The sand's brightness comes from oolitic aragonite, near-spherical grains of calcium carbonate that precipitate out of the warm, carbonate-saturated Bahama Banks water, not from crushed quartz.

Tourism took off in the 1950s, when the strip earned the nickname the Bahamian Riviera. The Emerald Beach Hotel opened in 1954 as the Bahamas' first air-conditioned hotel and its largest casino at the time; the site was later redeveloped as the Crystal Palace Resort, whose casino closed in February 2015, and the Wyndham/Crystal Palace towers were demolished in October 2018. Howard Johnson opened his first hotel outside the continental United States here in 1958. After independence in 1973, several hotels failed; the Pindling government bought them, and the Free National Movement re-privatized a number in the 1990s.

The complex dominating Cable Beach today is Baha Mar: 1,000 acres, roughly $4 billion, three brands — Grand Hyatt, SLS, Rosewood — 2,200 rooms, a 100,000-square-foot casino, a Jack Nicklaus golf course. Developer Sarkis Izmirlian began assembling the parcels in 2005 and broke ground on 21 February 2011, financed by a $2.45 billion China Exim Bank loan and built by state contractor China Construction America. Completion, targeted for late 2014, slipped to 27 March 2015.

That date was missed. BML Properties hit a liquidity crisis and filed Chapter 11 in June 2015 with the resort 97 percent finished; construction stopped for nearly a year. A China Exim Bank subsidiary took control in October 2016, and Hong Kong's Chow Tai Fook Enterprises bought the property outright that December. Baha Mar reopened in stages — Grand Hyatt in April 2017, SLS that November, Rosewood in June 2018 — six years after groundbreaking.

In October 2024, a New York judge ruled on what happened during the delay. Justice Andrew Borrok found China Construction America had committed fraud at least four times, describing "outright sabotage" of the project — including diverting a $54 million subcontractor payment to buy an unrelated hotel — and ordered it to pay BML Properties $1.6 billion. Cable Beach's skyline exists because a fight over who broke the project took nine years to settle, in a Manhattan courtroom rather than Nassau.
spike_explainer:
Cable Beach is a resort strip whose biggest building exists because a New York court eventually decided who wrecked it. That is not a metaphor. In October 2024, nine years after the resort now covering most of the beach was supposed to open, a Manhattan judge ruled that the Chinese state contractor hired to build it had committed fraud and "outright sabotage," and ordered it to pay $1.6 billion in damages.

**What was supposed to happen.** Bahamian-Armenian developer Sarkis Izmirlian began assembling Cable Beach parcels in 2005, aiming to replace aging properties on the strip — including the Crystal Palace Resort and the Nassau Beach Hotel — with a single mega-resort. He broke ground on 21 February 2011 on what became Baha Mar: eventually three hotel brands (Grand Hyatt, SLS, Rosewood), 2,200 rooms, a 100,000-square-foot casino, a Jack Nicklaus golf course, on 1,000 acres. The money came from the Export-Import Bank of China, $2.45 billion of it, and the general contractor was China Construction America (CCA), a subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction conglomerate. Completion was set for late 2014, then for 27 March 2015 — a date Izmirlian's company, BML Properties, announced publicly and staffed up to meet.

**What the court found actually happened.** Justice Andrew Borrok's 2024 ruling, in BML Properties' suit against CCA, laid out a specific pattern rather than ordinary delay. At a November 2014 meeting in Beijing, CCA told BML it needed $54 million urgently to pay subcontractors ahead of the March opening. BML wired it. CCA used the exact sum to buy the British Colonial Hilton, an unrelated Nassau hotel — what the judge called "an absolute sham and shakedown." Through January and February 2015, with six weeks left before the deadline, CCA pulled its head scheduler off Baha Mar and reassigned him to projects in Panama; the master schedule went unupdated for weeks. Roughly 700 Chinese workers were released to go home for Chinese New Year, from December 2014 into February 2015, without replacements lined up, while CCA kept telling BML the job was on track. Company executives, the ruling found, had also charged personal purchases — scarves, golf equipment, cigars — against project funds. Borrok concluded CCA breached its contractual "Best Interests Obligation" at least six times and committed fraud at least four times, actively working "to push BMLP out of the Project."

**What it cost Izmirlian.** The March 2015 deadline came and went. BML Properties, its cash exhausted, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in June 2015 with the resort reported at 97 percent complete. Construction stopped entirely for close to a year. In October 2016, Perfect Luck Holdings — a subsidiary of the same China Exim Bank that had financed the project — took control through the bankruptcy proceedings. Two months later, in December 2016, Hong Kong's Chow Tai Fook Enterprises bought the resort outright and finished it. Izmirlian, who had personally lost his firm's $845 million equity stake, put it bluntly afterward: he had conceived of Baha Mar more than twenty years earlier, "only to see it ripped out of my hands at the brink of opening by CCA." He filed suit in New York in December 2017, arguing the delay hadn't been mismanagement — it had been deliberate.

**What opened, and when.** Chow Tai Fook's version of Baha Mar opened in stages: Grand Hyatt in April 2017, SLS that November, Rosewood in June 2018 — a resort that had been sold to the public as opening in 2014, arriving three and a half years late under a different owner. It is, by any visitor's account, a functioning luxury complex now: a Nicklaus golf course, a convention center hosting the annual Bahamas Championship college basketball tournament since 2021, a full casino floor, three name-brand hotels running normally. None of that operational normalcy required the 2024 verdict to exist. The verdict addressed a separate, narrower question — not whether Baha Mar eventually worked, but who was responsible for it not working on schedule, and what that cost the man who started it.

**Why the number matters.** BML Properties' claimed damages started from its lost $845 million equity contribution, with interest accruing from a May 2014 breach date the court identified, compounding to $1.6 billion by the time of the 2024 ruling. That is a striking figure for a beach that most visitors experience as a stretch of pale sand in front of a casino. It is also, functionally, the only precise dollar accounting anyone has produced for what went wrong at Cable Beach's central redevelopment — a nine-year paper trail that ends with a state-owned Chinese contractor found, by a U.S. court, to have sabotaged the job it was paid $2.45 billion in Chinese state financing to complete. The beach did not change hands over geology or storms. It changed hands over a courtroom finding of fraud.
honest_reckoning_note:
The honest problem with Cable Beach's Baha Mar story is that its resolution looks cleaner than it was. A U.S. court found fraud, awarded $1.6 billion, and the resort now runs three full hotel brands — a tidy ending. But the $1.6 billion goes to BML Properties, the bankrupt entity Izmirlian no longer controls; Izmirlian himself, who spent two decades and $845 million of equity conceiving the project, does not own the beach he assembled. Baha Mar today belongs to Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, a Hong Kong jeweler-turned-conglomerate that bought it in 2016 for a fraction of what it cost to build, after the original financier's own subsidiary foreclosed on it. The court found who broke the deal. It did not undo who lost the beach.

The labor side of the story got less attention than the financial one. Roughly 70 percent of the Baha Mar construction workforce was brought in from mainland China rather than hired locally, and the 2024 ruling documents CCA sending roughly 700 of those workers home for Chinese New Year in the final months before the missed deadline, without arranging replacements — a staffing decision the court treated as evidence of sabotage, not simply of a foreign contractor's labor practices on Bahamian soil. Whatever the verdict changed about who owes whom, it did not retroactively create the Bahamian jobs a $4 billion project on Bahamian land might have been expected to generate during its five extra years under construction.
reckoning_pullquote: A New York court found who broke the deal — it did not return the beach to the man who built it.

margin_notes.text: Oolitic aragonite grains form as calcium carbonate precipitates out of warm, wave-agitated water and accretes in concentric layers around a nucleus, producing near-perfectly round grains rather than the angular quartz fragments of most temperate beaches.

The Emerald Beach Hotel's casino floor opened in 1954 as the Bahamas' largest at the time; the site was later redeveloped as the Crystal Palace Casino, which closed in February 2015, and the Wyndham/Crystal Palace towers were demolished in October 2018 — today's Baha Mar Casino is new construction built 2011-2017.

New Providence has recorded 18 tropical cyclone tracks within 50 nautical miles over the past 50 years, including at least one Category 5 system, per the NOAA IBTrACS archive — the reason hurricane season (June-November) shapes Cable Beach's resort booking calendar.

The $2.45 billion China Exim Bank loan made Baha Mar one of China's largest single overseas financing commitments in the Caribbean at the time — a scale of state lending that gave China Construction America outsized leverage once the project fell behind schedule.

Court records describe roughly 700 Chinese construction workers being released to return home for Chinese New Year between December 2014 and February 2015 — the final stretch before the missed March 2015 deadline — without replacement labor arranged.

Justice Borrok's ruling also found CCA executives had charged personal items, including scarves, golf equipment, and cigars, against Baha Mar project funds — a detail the court cited alongside the $54 million hotel-purchase diversion as evidence of bad faith.

day_in_time.dawn: Early morning on Cable Beach is dominated by resort staff shift changes at Baha Mar and joggers along West Bay Street; Baha Mar's casino floor — new construction built 2011-2017 — stays open around the clock, on a strip whose original 1954 casino site was redeveloped as the Crystal Palace Casino, which closed in 2015 before being demolished in 2018.
day_in_time.midday: By late morning the resort-front sections fill with hotel guests on loungers while the public access stretches see fewer visitors; the shallow, current-sheltered water off New Providence's lee shore stays calm enough for swimming without the surf found on the island's ocean-facing coasts.
day_in_time.golden: Late afternoon brings the golf course and beach-club crowd back toward the hotel towers; Cable Beach faces north rather than west, so the sunset itself plays out over the island behind the resorts rather than out over the water.
day_in_time.night: After dark, Baha Mar's casino floor carries the beach's nightlife; the sand itself empties out, patrolled by resort security rather than any public lifeguard service, and the glass towers built through the 2011-2018 construction saga stay lit over an otherwise dark shoreline.

food_drink.name: Baha Mar resort dining (Grand Hyatt, SLS, Rosewood)
food_drink.description: The three Baha Mar hotel brands each operate their own restaurant slate on-property; this is the primary sit-down dining directly on the Cable Beach frontage.
food_drink.where: Baha Mar resort complex, Cable Beach

food_drink.name: Conch salad and cracked conch at the Arawak Cay "Fish Fry"
food_drink.description: A cluster of local seafood shacks on West Bay Street known for conch prepared raw in citrus (salad) or battered and fried (cracked); it is not on Cable Beach itself but sits along the same road toward downtown Nassau.
food_drink.where: Arawak Cay, West Bay Street, roughly a 10-minute drive east of Cable Beach

food_drink.name: Kalik beer and Goombay Smash
food_drink.description: Kalik is the Bahamas' domestically brewed lager; the Goombay Smash is a rum-based cocktail associated with Bahamian beach bars generally, both served at Cable Beach's resort bars.

food_drink.name: Rum cake
food_drink.description: A dense, rum-soaked cake sold as a Bahamian specialty, especially around the holidays, at resort gift shops and bakeries near the hotel strip.
food_drink.where: Gift shops and bakeries near Cable Beach resorts

timeline.title: Telegraph cable lands at Goodman's Bay
timeline.description: A submarine telegraph cable from Jupiter, Florida comes ashore at Goodman's Bay, the first cable link between the Bahamas and the United States, giving the beach its name.

timeline.title: Emerald Beach Hotel opens
timeline.description: The Emerald Beach Hotel opens as the first air-conditioned hotel in the Bahamas and the country's largest casino at the time; the site was later redeveloped as the Crystal Palace Casino, which closed in February 2015, and the towers were demolished in October 2018.

timeline.title: Howard Johnson opens first international hotel
timeline.description: Howard Deering Johnson opens his chain's first hotel outside the continental United States on Cable Beach.

timeline.title: Izmirlian begins assembling Baha Mar parcels
timeline.description: Bahamian-Armenian developer Sarkis Izmirlian begins acquiring Cable Beach properties, including the Crystal Palace Resort and Nassau Beach Hotel sites, for what becomes Baha Mar.
timeline.source: Global Construction Review / NY Supreme Court ruling summary

timeline.title: Baha Mar breaks ground
timeline.description: Construction begins on Baha Mar on 21 February 2011, financed by a $2.45 billion China Exim Bank loan and built by China Construction America.

timeline.title: Missed opening triggers bankruptcy filing
timeline.description: The 27 March 2015 completion date is missed with the resort roughly 97% complete; developer BML Properties files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in Delaware that June, and construction halts for close to a year starting in April 2016.

timeline.title: Chow Tai Fook acquires Baha Mar
timeline.description: Hong Kong's Chow Tai Fook Enterprises agrees to buy Baha Mar from China Exim Bank on 14 December 2016, after the bank's subsidiary Perfect Luck Holdings took control of the bankrupt project that October.

timeline.title: Baha Mar reopens under new ownership
timeline.description: The Grand Hyatt at Baha Mar opens in April 2017 under Chow Tai Fook ownership and management, the first of the resort's three hotel brands to open; SLS follows that November.

timeline.title: NY court orders CCA to pay $1.6 billion for fraud
timeline.description: Justice Andrew Borrok of the New York State Supreme Court rules that China Construction America committed fraud and "outright sabotage" against BML Properties during the Baha Mar build, ordering $1.6 billion in damages.
timeline.source: Global Construction Review, "Outright sabotage: Why a judge ordered China Construction America to pay $1.6bn"

zones.name: Baha Mar frontage
zones.character: The beach frontage of the 1,000-acre Baha Mar complex — Grand Hyatt, SLS, and Rosewood hotels, the 100,000-square-foot casino, and beach-club infrastructure built between 2011 and 2018.
zones.best_for: Resort-guest beach access, casino, organized water sports
zones.notes: Sits on land assembled from 2005 onward, including the former Crystal Palace Resort and Nassau Beach Hotel sites. On Baha Mar's eastern flank (toward downtown Nassau), the former Meliá Nassau Beach (originally the Sheraton Nassau Beach Resort) closed in 2021 and was demolished in 2024; the cleared site is slated to become Baha Mar's fourth hotel, planned to open in 2029.

zones.name: West Cable Beach resort cluster
zones.character: The stretch west of Baha Mar fronting Sandals Royal Bahamian, predating the Baha Mar redevelopment.

zones.name: Public beach access points
zones.character: Sand between and around resort properties remains publicly walkable at the waterline; several informal access points off West Bay Street let non-guests reach the water without a resort day pass.

zones.name: Goodman's Bay (cable landing site)
zones.character: The eastern approach toward downtown Nassau, near where the 1892 telegraph cable came ashore and gave the beach its name; today a mix of parkland and roadway rather than resort frontage.
zones.notes: Coordinates approximate; marks the historical cable landing area rather than a precise surveyed point.

things_to_know.label: Multiple owners, no single entrance
things_to_know.note: Cable Beach frontage is split between Baha Mar, Sandals Royal Bahamian, the demolished former Meliá Nassau Beach site (awaiting a planned Baha Mar hotel targeted for 2029), and public access points; there is no single formal entrance, and resort sections can require a day pass or room key.

things_to_know.label: The sand is oolitic, not quartz
things_to_know.note: The pale, fine sand is oolitic aragonite — round carbonate grains formed in the surrounding banks — rather than the crushed quartz found on most continental beaches.

things_to_know.label: Hurricane season shapes the calendar
things_to_know.note: New Providence has recorded 18 tropical cyclone tracks within 50 nautical miles over the past 50 years, including at least one Category 5 storm; June through November is hurricane season.

things_to_know.label: Airport is close but not adjacent
things_to_know.note: Lynden Pindling International Airport (NAS) is about 7.5 km away in a straight line, but the road route via West Bay Street runs roughly 9 km (5.5 mi), a 12-15 minute drive.

access_note: Cable Beach fronts West Bay Street on New Providence's north shore, about 9 km (5.5 mi) by road from Lynden Pindling International Airport (NAS) — a 12-15 minute drive. Downtown Nassau is about 8 km (10-12 min) east by road (6.4 km straight-line). The beach is a mix of resort-controlled frontage (Baha Mar, Sandals Royal Bahamian, and the demolished former Meliá Nassau Beach site, awaiting a planned Baha Mar hotel targeted for 2029) and public access points off West Bay Street; there is no single formal entrance.
